items.title: James Hunter interviewed by Monk Rowe, Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018
items.q: So I went for that initially because a lot of the New Orleans rhythm & blues stuff I was listening to like Guitar Slim, Edgar Blanchard, was using this doubled up tenor and baritone playing octaves apart

ctx.x: Yeah. It’s nice if you have to look for it, I like that. I also wondered, how did you settle, or maybe it wasn’t settling, but with two tenors, or the tenor and the baritone, rather than, if you had an alto and a trumpet your band would sound a lot different.

It would be different. I mean the thing is, the reason I initially went for that is cause you could get the most range, or the most variety of sounds between the two. So I went for that initially because a lot of the New Orleans rhythm & blues stuff I was listening to like Guitar Slim, Edgar Blanchard, was using this doubled up tenor and baritone playing octaves apart so which give it a sort of fat spectrum of sound. But my idea was to not always just keep it to that, but to get as much variety as I could. And so…
Oh you’ve got one melody that you’re singing and the saxes are —
